newsitem.title: SWEDEN: ATHLETICS-ENGQUIST SAYS TONGUE NOT LEGS HOLDING HER BACK.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-ENGQUIST SAYS TONGUE NOT LEGS HOLDING HER BACK.

text.p: Ludmila Engquist, the adopted darling of Swedish athletics, says her tongue, not her legs, is holding her back.

The Russian-born runner, who was made a Swedish citizen just weeks before taking gold in the 100 metre hurdles at the last year's Atlanta Olympics, said making herself understood was her biggest hurdle and a psychological barrier to her performance.
"When I become good in Swedish I will be able to run better," Engquist said in an interview in the lobby of a Stockholm hotel attached to the city's top sporting arena.
The 32-year-old world record holder, who was born in Tambov, southeast of Moscow, said lack of time stopped her from formally studying Swedish or English.
Currently at the peak of her athletics career, Engquist is completely focused on her track performance.

With two world records under her belt -- one set in 1990 in the 60 metre hurdles at 7.69 seconds and another in the 100 metre indoor hurdles in which she clocked 12.64 in February -- Engquist is going for the hatrick.
"There's only one left, the 100 metres outdoor hurdles," said the quietly spoken athlete who is the only Swedish women ever to win an Olympics athletics medal.
"My goal is to run fast, to break world records...to win as many competitions as possible."

Engquist said a constant battle for perfection had been her driving force over the past few years in which she has struggled through a doping ban, marital difficulties and moved from her homeland of Russia to a new life in Sweden.

Three years ago, while still running for Russia, Engquist was locked in a legal battle with sporting authorities. She had been banned from competing for four years after a positive drugs test at Lievin, France.

However the ban was cut short in December 1995 after a determined Engquist, then running as Ludmila Narozhilenko, successfully argued that her estranged former husband spiked her drink with steroids in an attempt to destroy her career.
Her ex-husband came forward and confessed and the ban was lifted by the International Amateur Athletic Federation.
Now remarried to her Swedish trainer, Johan, Ludmila and her teenager daughter Natasha have made Sweden their home, living in Stockholm.
The golden-haired athlete, who has been elevated to celebrity status in Sweden since her Olympic win and is featured extensively in Swedish magazines, said she had been made welcome in Sweden.
Every week she receives piles of fan mail and this year was awarded a Swedish prize given to the year's best athlete based on votes by members of the public.
"There are not so many countries where people accept other people so easily," said Engquist in her heavily-accented Swedish.
"I understand that people accept me and think highly of me. When I'm nostalgic it's because I want to speak Russian.
"Nearly all my friends were athletes and I still see them at competitions."
Engquist said she finds losing hard to bear.
"When I lose a race I think not only about myself, but about what others will think of me. I can't look people into the eyes," said Engquist.
"I understand I will lose many competitions, but I don't want to and I don't want to disappoint people."
After her triumphs last year, 1997 has been mixed for Engquist.

She set the 100 metre indoor hurdles before suffering a hamstring injury which barred her from an indoor competition in Stockholm and kept her out of the world indoor championships in Paris last weekend.
But the resilient Engquist said she expected to be back in action for this summer's outdoor season which is more important to her.
At the end of March Engquist will travel to Spain to follow a rigorous six day a week training schedule.
She will kick off the outdoor season in June with a six-week period concentrating on speed.
"It means we're not going to do so many competitions but they will be in places where we know there are good conditions and fast tracks to try and be close to the world outdoor record," said Johan.
"When that phase is over by mid-July there will be three weeks of concentration for the world championships in Athens."
